items.summary: Trump dismisses concerns over conditions on US aircraft carrier President Donald Trump dismissed concerns Friday over living conditions and the mental health of service members on a US aircraft carrier deployed against Iran and said the ship would soon rotate out. Asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation on the Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, Trump said: "No, they're not." Trump also rejected that the ship - now in its ninth month at sea - had been deployed for too long. "No, no, no, not nearly enough," he said. Trump confirmed reports that the Abraham Lincoln was due to be rotated with a replacement aircraft carrier as the United States remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz and the country's nuclear programme. "That ship is moving right now or very shortly, and it's being replaced with another very similar ship," Trump said.

items.title: Iran says Hormuz transit route deal reached with Oman
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz transit route deal reached with Oman Iran on Monday said it has reached an understanding with Oman on a plan for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz, with the two sides now working to finalise details and issue a joint statement. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said “an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route”, adding that the agreement was being prepared as a package including the route map. Details that have previously emerged suggest ships could enter the strait along a route close to Iran and exit near Oman, without paying fees or tolls during an interim period. Baghaei acknowledged that negotiations had moved slowly but said Tehran and Muscat still planned to finalise the arrangement, as a deadline for a broader agreement between the United States and Iran expired without a deal.

items.title: Iran says talks with Oman continue on new Hormuz transit route
items.summary: Iran says talks with Oman continue on new Hormuz transit route Iran and Oman are continuing talks to establish a secure maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said, blaming security complications caused by US and Israeli military actions. “Drawing up the maritime transit route plan with Oman has been time-consuming due to security complexities,” Baghaei said, adding that “the issue is inherently complex”. Speaking on the proposed mechanism, Baghaei said it would aim to protect the sovereign rights and interests of both Iran and Oman while ensuring the safe passage of commercial vessels. “This is the first time that a mechanism is being developed to simultaneously safeguard the sovereign rights of the two littoral states and ensure the safe passage of commercial vessels,” he said, adding that intensive talks to finalise a joint statement were continuing.

items.summary: Qatar says Hormuz agreement crucial for US-Iran talks to resume Qatar has said that an agreement between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz would make it easier to resume negotiations to end the Iran war. Iran and Oman, both coastal states bordering the Strait of Hormuz, have for weeks been discussing the future of navigation through the waterway, with Tehran saying the geographical coordinates of the route envisaged by both countries "have been agreed upon". "We are also awaiting an agreement between the Sultanate of Oman and Iran regarding the Strait, which would enable us to return to the framework of negotiations," Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters. "The agreement over the Strait of Hormuz would make it much easier for us to resume the talks between the United States and Iran," he added. A memorandum of understanding signed between the two sides in June effectively collapsed over management of the strait. items.title: Iran resumes flights at Bandar Abbas airport after wartime disruptions
items.summary: Iran resumes flights at Bandar Abbas airport after wartime disruptions Flights at the port city of Bandar Abbas resumed on Saturday after repeated interruptions during war with the United States, state media reported. Kazem Tavassoli, director general of airports in Hormozgan province, said "scheduled flights at Bandar Abbas International Airport on high-traffic domestic routes resumed today, according to the IRNA state news agency. The reopening comes "following limited flights in recent days", Tavassoli said, adding that passengers can now buy tickets for the Tehran-Bandar Abbas, Mashhad-Bandar Abbas and Bandar Abbas-Isfahan routes, in both directions. The airport "handled 35 to 40 domestic and international flights per day" before the war, Tavassoli said. The airport has been repeatedly closed since the United States launched its war on Iran.

Des déclarations en réplique à celles de Donald Trump qui affirmait qu'après la guerre, il ferait du détroit d'Ormuz un territoire américain. Le 14 août a été marqué par ailleurs par plusieurs attaques, dan ce détroit, notamment celle d'un pétrolier de la compagnie émiratie Adnoc. De leur côté, les Houthis, basés au Yémen, ont revendiqué une nouvelle frappe de drone contre un site du géant pétrolier Aramco, situé dans le sud-ouest de l'Arabie saoudite. items.summary: Iran says 60-day deadline under US deal is no longer relevant Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said a 60-day period linked to the 17 June memorandum between Tehran and Washington was no longer relevant, accusing the United States of violating the agreement weeks after it was signed. “There is no provision in the memorandum of understanding referring to a ‘60-day deadline’, and the Islamic Republic of Iran never formulates its policies under pressure, ultimatums or time limits,” he said. Baghaei said the memorandum envisaged a 60-day period for talks on “the lifting of sanctions” and “the nuclear issue”, which could have been extended if no agreement was reached. However, he said “gross and widespread” US violations meant talks never began. “As a result, the issue of a 60-day deadline became entirely moot,” Baghaei added.

Vessels used the Iranian side of the strait or undermined routes, “while no crossings were recorded through the Hormuz TSS or Omani routes”, Kpler posted on X. items.title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi military ship in Red Sea
items.summary: Houthis say they targeted Saudi military ship in Red Sea Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday that they had targeted a Saudi military vessel and four escort ships in the Red Sea with missiles. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree announced the attack on Telegram. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities. The reported attack comes days after the Houthis targeted a vessel near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Yemen’s transport ministry said four crew members were killed in that attack. The Bab el-Mandeb is a strategic maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for international shipping. In July, the Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, accusing Riyadh of imposing a siege on Yemen. Saudi Arabia has denied the allegation.

clusters.headline: Iran bars two French diplomats from returning

items.title: Iran bars two French diplomats from returning
items.summary: Iran bars two French diplomats from returning Iran said on Monday that two French diplomats briefly arrested last month over alleged “interference” would not be allowed to return to the country. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said the pair had left Iran and that Tehran had formally informed France they would be barred from re-entry. France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on 20 July that the diplomats had been targeted by Iranian security officials in violation of diplomatic immunity and described the incident as an “extremely serious act of intimidation”. Iran has accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs while engaging with civil society. Its intelligence ministry said they were involved in a broader effort to exert foreign influence, without providing further details. Tehran summoned the French ambassador on 26 July to protest against the diplomats’ conduct. Baqaei said on Monday that French authorities should apologise, arguing that the pair had violated the Vienna Convention.

items.summary: Iranian parliament advances bill to curb foreign influence Iran's parliament approved on Sunday the general principles of a bill that would criminalise interviews and other communications with media deemed hostile to the Islamic Republic, including US or Israeli media and outlets financed by either country, Iran's Shargh newspaper reported. Osman Salari, a member of parliament's judicial and legal commission, said the individual provisions of the bill, which is aimed at countering foreign intelligence influence, have yet to be debated and approved. Reports about the bill's details should not be considered final yet, Salari told the Mizan news agency. Under the proposed bill, interviews or participation in discussions with such media would be banned, with violations punishable by six months to two years in prison. items.summary: Araghchi says talks with Oman about Strait of Hormuz ‘may reach conclusion soon’ Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that negotiations between Iran and Oman “may reach a conclusion soon,” Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) reported. Araghchi said the talks with Oman regarding the shared management of the Strait of Hormuz between the two countries “are ongoing, but this is a completely separate discussion” from ceasefire talks with the United States. He added that “a technical discussion related to determining the maritime routes of the Strait of Hormuz for ship traffic” is continuing. “This is a technical work that is being done between experts from the two countries and the armed forces are also involved in it,” Araghchi said. “In any case, they are the main opinion leaders on this issue.”

Valiullah Bayati, a spokesperson for the parliament’s internal affairs and councils committee, said on Friday that the proposals would now advance for further consideration. “The strategic action plan to ensure the security and progress of the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf was reviewed by the Councils’ Commission and, after hearing the opinions, its general outline was approved,” said Bayati to the Tasnim news agency . The plan would prevent vessels and equipment belonging to the US, Israel and other countries Iran designates as hostile from passing through the waterway. items.title: Iran Defiant as Trump Tells Americans to Accept High Gas Prices
Trump urges Americans to accept higher oil prices
items.summary: Trump urges Americans to accept higher oil prices US President Donald Trump has urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices as the cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The comments underscore the growing political risk for Trump as higher fuel prices collide with his campaign promise to lower energy costs, with Democrats already seeking to make the economic fallout from the Iran war an issue heading into the November midterm elections. In a speech in Garden City, Trump said Americans who had to "pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" should remember that this was the cost of ensuring "a very evil country" could not have a nuclear weapon. "What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a great job," said Trump, adding he would never apologize for attacking Iran. Around roughly 20 percent of global oil and LNG shipments usually pass through the Strait of Hormuz and the potential for long-term disruption has pushed up oil prices. (Reporting by Reuters)

items.title: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade
items.summary: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade The price of Brent North Sea crude, the main international oil contract, climbed above $90 on Tuesday as hopes that the US and Iran reach a deal to end the war fade. Brent reached $90.02 a barrel, a gain of more than 2.5 percent from Monday, while the main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, jumped 2.7 percent to $84.32 a barrel. Crude has surged more than 10 percent over the past week, with the US and Iran appearing no closer to a deal on the Strait of Hormuz despite optimistic comments from Washington earlier this month. In the latest blow, Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek conflict compensation from Iran as part of any peace negotiations, responding to Tehran's own demand for US war reparations as a condition of any deal.

clusters.headline: Houthis may meet their match as Yemen slips back into civil war

items.title: Houthis may meet their match as Yemen slips back into civil war
items.summary: Yemen’s front lines have barely moved since the 2022 truce, but the war around them is changing. Ballistic missiles and drones are striking far beyond established positions, and forces associated with the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government are responding more aggressively to infiltrations and military buildups. As commanders review readiness across key fronts, Yemen’s political leadership is signaling that attacks will no longer be absorbed without a response. Together, the developments suggest that the country’s long period of “no war, no peace” may be coming to an end. There has been no ground offensive large enough to redraw the map so far. But war can return gradually as long-range strikes increase, forces reinforce positions and the rules of retaliation begin to change. Mokha: War without taking territory The Port of Mokha stopped operating two weeks ago amid repeated Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks. Maandenlang was het relatief rustig in de hoofdstad Khartoem. Sinds het leger de stad vorig jaar weer in handen kreeg , proberen inwoners er een nieuw leven op te bouwen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf linked the shift to two commanders assassinated by the United States in January 2020. “Dear Abu Mahdi and Haj Qassem! An alliance official said on Wednesday that NATO would confront any danger and take whatever action it considered necessary to protect its members. "As demonstrated earlier this year when NATO air defences successfully intercepted ballistic missiles heading to Turkey from Iran on four separate occasions, our deterrence and defence posture is strong and effective," the official said. Este último sondeo de Reuters/Ipsos muestra que Trump cae todavía respecto a su última lectura, a comienzos de agosto, cuando su aprobación estaba en el 35%. Y llega en la recta final de la temporada de primarias -esta noche del martes se votaba, por ejemplo, en Florida y Alaska - y a solo un mes de que los estadounidenses empiecen a votar de forma anticipada para renovar el Congreso.Los números de Trump son inseparables de la guerra de Irán

clusters.headline: Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On…

items.title: Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On…
items.summary: The Iran war is beginning to resemble the Ukraine war in one important way. Operationally, the wars themselves are still very different — Ukraine is a large-scale ground invasion, while the Iran war is not there just yet. But their political logic after a failure to achieve a quick result is starting to look very similar. In both cases, a larger power expected its overwhelming military force to produce a quick political result. And in both cases, that expectation failed.The targeted state adapted, outside supporters helped it remain afloat, and both conflicts moved from the promise of a decisive outcome The post Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On… appeared first on War on the Rocks .

clusters.headline: US Justice Department targets Iranian institute for activity linked to IRGC

items.title: US Justice Department targets Iranian institute for activity linked to IRGC
items.summary: US Justice Department targets Iranian institute for activity linked to IRGC The US Department of Justice (DoJ) announced charges on Tuesday against 17 members of Iran’s Mabna Institute for cyber activity and hacking “carried out on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other Iranian entities”. In a statement, the Department said Mabna Institute was involved in “a widespread cyber campaign”, which targeted over than 100,000 accounts belonging to university professors worldwide and stole more than 31 terabytes of academic and intellectual property data, along with email accounts belonging to employees. The campaign targeted 144 US universities and 178 foreign universities, at least 42 US companies and 11 foreign companies, as well as at least five US federal and local government agencies and two nongovernmental organisations, resulting in costs exceeding $20m, according to the statement.

items.summary: US mulls shrinking military footprint in Gulf as a result of war on Iran: Report The Trump administration is examining whether to pull troops out of the Gulf as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, with the Pentagon weighing the risks facing large US bases in the region that have come under Iranian drone and missile attack. The evaluation is being led by the Department of War’s policy office, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday, saying the war was viewed as “a once-in-a-generation chance for the Pentagon to reconsider its presence in the region”. The report said that the US has already signalled that it might not rebuild its bases attacked by Iran to pre-war status. The Washington Post corroborates Middle East Eye’s June report that cited current and former US officials as saying that a reckoning with the US’s old basing framework was expected as a result of the war. Former senior US officials have raised the prospect of a drawdown for months. items.summary: Los mercados empiezan a asumir una realidad que Donald Trump se resiste a reconocer : la paz en el Golfo Pérsico no llegará pronto y sus consecuencias económicas pueden agravarse durante las próximas semanas. El petróleo ha vuelto a subir, mientras las rentabilidades de la deuda pública alcanzan máximos de muchos años en Estados Unidos y varias economías europeas. El bono norteamericano a 30 años, un elemento clave de las carteras de renta fija a nivel mundial, está en su nivel más elevado desde 2007. Los inversores descuentan ya el riesgo de que la energía cara prolongue la inflación y obligue a mantener elevados los tipos de interés. Casi seis meses después, ha expirado sin resultados el plazo de sesenta días del memorándum firmado el 17 de junio. items.summary: On Tuesday, Israel bombed a Syrian airbase that Turkish officials have been helping to renovate, marking the latest escalation in the Israeli government’s effort to beat back Turkey’s influence in Syria. The strikes, which reportedly damaged an airstrip and a storage facility at the Abu al-Duhur Airbase, did not lead to any casualties. Still, they drew a strong rebuke from U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack, a long-time friend of President Donald Trump who is also serving as the president’s envoy to Syria. Still, the ensuing war has followed a clear, predictable logic. After decades of sanctions failed to persuade Iranians to overthrow the regime, Israel and the U.S. resorted to war; after that failed too, they turned to a naval blockade. Each escalation has had an impact, adding to the misery of life in Iran, but so far each has missed its ultimate target: forcing a surrender. items.title: China es ahora la gran potencia petrolera mundial
items.summary: La guerra de Irán ha provocado la mayor crisis de suministro de la historia del petróleo. Ni siquiera en los momentos más intensos de los combates los precios del petróleo alcanzaron los 150 dólares por barril que muchos analistas habían pronosticado al inicio del conflicto. Esto se lo debemos agradecer a algunos gobiernos. Poco después de que las municiones iraníes hicieran intransitable el estrecho de Ormuz, dejando atrapados 14 millones de barriles al día de crudo en el Golfo, los monarcas petroleros de Abu Dabi y Riad desviaron 5 millones de barriles al día adicionales a través de oleoductos que eludían el estrecho. Los ministros de Washington y Tokio liberaron una cantidad récord de 2 millones de barriles al día de reservas de emergencia; el racionamiento impuesto por el Estado en los países más pobres redujo considerablemente la demanda.Sin embargo, la catástrofe se habría producido de todos modos sin las decisiones tomadas discretamente en otra capital: Pekín. clusters.headline: The Iran war flushed $1.3 billion of Reaper drones down the drain

items.title: The Iran war flushed $1.3 billion of Reaper drones down the drain
items.summary: The U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, worth at least $1.3 billion, since the start of its war on Iran, the Washington Post reported Friday . The drones can cost between $30 and $50 million each, depending on their sensor and weapons payload. The U.S. military has lost roughly 25% of its pre-war fleet in the past five months. A defense official told the Washington Post that some of the drones were not shot down by Iranian forces, but instead were lost after their communications link to their operators failed. They did not say how many were lost this way. items.title: Pentagon signs multibillion-dollar Tomahawk deal amid missile shortage concerns
items.summary: Pentagon signs multibillion-dollar Tomahawk deal amid missile shortage concerns The Pentagon announced a $22.9bn contract with Raytheon on Monday to accelerate deliveries of Tomahawk missiles, amid reports that US missile stocks have been strained by the war with Iran. Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the deal would speed up deliveries “at unprecedented speed” to meet current operational demands. A recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that US stocks of Patriot and THAAD interceptors have been cut by roughly half or more since the conflict with Iran began in late February. The Washington Post also reported that President Donald Trump had pressed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth for answers over munitions shortages, though both later denied that US missile stocks were running low. Tomahawk missiles are launched mainly from submarines and warships and have a range of more than 1,600km.

items.summary: The United States has always asked extraordinary things of its service members. But this week, a series of remarkable news stories came out documenting the dire conditions of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln , a ship that has been at sea so long that those aboard have not stepped foot on land since 2025. Even families like mine, who have experienced multiple combat deployments, are alarmed by the depictions we read in this news. clusters.headline: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026

items.title: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026
items.summary: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026 As the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, Iran struck back near US military installations in the Gulf, including in Qatar and the UAE. Several international airports were hit by Iranian strikes, including Dubai, the world's busiest for international passengers, as well as Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Bahrain. The UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait closed their airspaces due to safety concerns, gradually reopening them a week later as hostilities lessened. The war has had long-lasting consequences for regional aviation: falling passenger and cargo demand, fewer private jet flights, and global repercussions from high jet fuel prices. The International Air Transport Association's (IATA) June outlook estimated that airlines operating from the Middle East will see a $7.2bn net profit in 2025 become a $4.3bn net loss in 2026. items.title: Morale on US aircraft carrier enforcing Iran blockade plummets, as sailor jumps overboard: Report
items.summary: Morale on US aircraft carrier enforcing Iran blockade plummets, as sailor jumps overboard: Report The US is set to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier with the USS George Washington in the Middle East after reports of deteriorating conditions on the aircraft carrier enforcing a blockade of Iran . The Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days without a port call. At least one sailor jumped overboard the vessel, and another had to be restrained from doing so, according to media reports. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Lincoln will be rotated out of the theatre of operations and replaced with the USS George Washington. US lawmakers have raised concerns about the physical and mental health of sailors on board. The rotation comes after US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said that the blockade of Iran can be conducted “indefinitely”, as fighting continues to rage for control over the Strait of Hormuz with no return to a ceasefire in sight. items.summary: Most people associate the insects with filth, but they are vital to the food cycle and sometimes even pretty Vote for your favourite invertebrate Every spring, billions of flies commute thousands of miles in a huge web around the world. They may begin life in Iran and then spend the rest of it in the UK. They may hatch in India but undertake seasonal migrations to the fertile regions of Mongolia, China and Siberia. Most of us assume that bees carry out pollination. But look closely at the creatures flitting around our gardens and parks, and you will see that many of those “bees” aren’t bees at all. items.summary: Assessment that has found a jump in UK productivity emphasises urgent need to appoint a national statistician The keen new chancellor, John Healey, responded to last week’s better-than-expected economic news by claiming the government was “bringing hope back”. items.summary: Opinion: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East Nearly three years after the 7 October Hamas attack shattered the illusion of a manageable status quo - one serving US - Israeli interests, while harming Palestinian rights - and midway through President Donald Trump’s second term, the Middle East no longer maps neatly onto the two axes that have defined it for decades. The region’s fault line long ran between Iran ’s “Axis of Resistance” - comprising Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi armed groups, and a battered but defiant Syria under the Assad regime - and the Israeli-inspired “Pax Americana”: an informal architecture of deterrence, normalisation, and military primacy that Washington and Tel Aviv sought to impose through the Abraham Accords, blatant double standards, international law violations and overwhelming force. Today, a third pole could be emerging: an increasingly institutionalised “Sunni axis” anchored in Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad - with Doha, Cairo, and to a lesser extent Abu Dhabi at its edges. items.title: Iran says route through Hormuz agreed with Oman, but deal yet to be finalised
items.summary: Iran says route through Hormuz agreed with Oman, but deal yet to be finalised Iran has reached an agreement with Oman on a shipping route map for the Strait of Hormuz after weeks of technical negotiations, Defa Press reported, citing Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. “Despite US obstruction, the talks have made positive progress over the past three weeks and an agreement has been reached on the shipping route map.” Baghaei added that both sides were still negotiating outstanding issues, including a statement to be issued by Tehran and Muscat. The Iran-Oman arrangement is an independent agreement aimed at ensuring the safe passage of ships through the strait, while respecting the sovereignty of both countries, he said.

items.summary: Iran accuses French diplomats of 'infiltration' The Iranian government has accused two French diplomats of conducting an "infiltration and interference" operation inside Iran. Iran's intelligence ministry alleged in a statement that the diplomats were discovered at a secret meeting place, and that documents found there pointed to efforts to establish contacts and build networks elsewhere. The ministry did not provide evidence for the claims, and the French government has not yet commented.

Ondanks het staakt-het-vuren voert Israël er bijna dagelijks aanvallen uit. items.title: Oman, la petroliera perde greggio in mare: dall’alto la chiazza nera di 2mila km quadrati
items.summary: Le immagini aeree diffuse da Oman TV mostrano il greggio fuoriuscire dalla Caroline Bezengi, petroliera incagliata al largo dell’isola di Al-Qibliyyah, nell’arcipelago delle Hallaniyat. La nave trasportava circa 800 mila barili di petrolio russo e la chiazza avrebbe ormai superato i 2 mila chilometri quadrati, raggiungendo anche la costa dell’Oman. L’incidente minaccia una riserva marina protetta, habitat tra l’altro delle megattere del Mar Arabico e dei cormorani di Socotra. La petroliera aveva segnalato problemi l’8 giugno dopo una possibile esplosione e si era poi arenata il 30 giugno; al momento l’episodio non è stato collegato alla guerra con l’Iran.

clusters.headline: Morning recap

items.title: Morning recap
items.summary: Morning recap Good morning Middle East Eye readers, President Donald Trump said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz part of US territory after defeating Iran. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi retorted that Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force by Washington. Trump’s remarks came as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said no decision has yet been made to resume negotiations with the United States. Araghchi added that mediator Qatar and Pakistan were in contact with Iran and exchanging messages, but that this did not amount to negotiations. Here are the latest developments from across the region: •    Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon early Saturday morning killed at least seven people. Advancing Israeli forces also demolished homes in Bint Jbeil. •    A bulk carrier has been struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz,  the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. •    Yemen’s government says at least four civilians were killed when Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of al-Mokha on Friday.

items.title: Morning update

items.title: Oil climbs over $1 a barrel as expert warns of ‘day of reckoning’
items.summary: Oil climbs over $1 a barrel as expert warns of ‘day of reckoning’ Crude oil futures climbed over $1 a barrel on tanker attacks and a lack of progress on a peace agreement between the US and Iran. Reuters reported that Brent futures settled at $88.52 a barrel, up $1.45, or 1.67percent. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures finished at $82.40, up $1.15, or 1.42 percent. Brent and WTI were on track for weekly gains of 6.0 percent and 5.4 percent, respectively. "We're getting a rally going into the weekend after new attacks on tankers and lack of progress on a cease-fire agreement," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Reuters. A "day of reckoning" may come if traffic in the strait of Hormuz remains constrained, Lipow said. "Crude oil prices might be $80 a barrel, but diesel prices are $180 a barrel and gasoline is $130 a barrel and that's what's hitting the consumer," he added.

items.summary: Hormuz traffic rises from nine to 13 crossings, Kpler says Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz increased on 13 August, with 13 confirmed vessel crossings, up 44 percent from nine crossings recorded the previous day, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. Nine vessels used Iran's unilateral transit scheme, while no vessels were confirmed on the Hormuz Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS). The routes of four other vessels remained undetermined. Activity through the Bab el-Mandeb was steadier, with 29 confirmed crossings, up 4 percent from 28 the previous day. Eighteen vessels entered the Red Sea and 11 exited, while two dark transits were recorded. No new confirmed vessel attacks were reported during the day, Kpler added. clusters.headline: Vance says low oil prices are top US goal in Iran conflict

items.title: Vance says low oil prices are top US goal in Iran conflict
items.summary: Vance says low oil prices are top US goal in Iran conflict Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that the top US priority in the Iran war was keeping oil and gasoline prices low for Americans, with preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon ranking second. The remarks contrasted with President Donald Trump's repeated framing of the fight: that entering the war had the sole objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, even if that meant short-term economic sacrifices for Americans. Vance's comments also underscored the growing reality that the war now centres on control of the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has forced to the top of the negotiating agenda. "I know that oil is down today and it's way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict," Vance said on Fox News. "That's goal number one - keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country." "And then obviously goal number two is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon," he added.

items.title: US has lost roughly 25 percent of its Reaper drones in Iran war: Report
items.summary: US has lost roughly 25 percent of its Reaper drones in Iran war: Report The US-Israeli war on Iran has depleted or destroyed more than $1.3bn worth of the US's MQ-9 Reaper drones, roughly translating to 25 percent of the country's pre-war fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a report by The Washington Post published on Friday. The report underscores how Iran's air defences have continued to be operational despite claims by President Donald Trump and his aides that they have been obliterated. The Washington Post story reveals a slightly higher number of MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed compared to a Bloomberg report published in May, which put the figure at 20 percent of the pre-war inventory. The MQ-9 Reaper drone is valued between $30m and $50m, depending on its sensor, radar, and ordnance configuration. The unmanned aerial vehicle serves as a high-altitude platform for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeted precision strikes, as documented by the US Air Force . items.title: Nederlandse economie veerkrachtig, maar de koopkracht gaat volgend jaar wel omlaag
items.summary: Door de oorlog in Iran en de hogere energieprijzen dreigen veel Nederlandse huishoudens in 2027 minder te besteden te krijgen. De koopkracht daalt met 0,3 procent als de overheid het beleid ongewijzigd laat. Dit jaar stijgt de koopkracht voor de doorsnee Nederlander nog wel, maar een stuk minder dan tot nu toe werd verwacht. In de laatste berekening ging het CBP er nog van uit dat dit jaar de koopkracht met 1,4 procent zou stijgen. Dat is bijgesteld naar 0,6 procent. Dat blijkt uit de nieuwste ramingen van het Centraal Planbureau (CPB) in de Macro-Economische Verkenningen (MEV). Die worden gezien als het uitgangspunt voor de onderhandelingen tussen politieke partijen over de Miljoenennota. Het kabinet kan, in samenwerking met de oppositie, maatregelen nemen om bepaalde groepen te compenseren. Toch vallen de gevolgen mee als je ziet wat er aan de hand is in de wereld, stelt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Over de hele linie valt het mee. De Nederlandse economie is veerkrachtig." items.title: Sen. Van Hollen: Iran war is illegal and we cannot fund another dime
items.summary: Today, there is no all-out war, no peace, and no light at the end of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump administration’s crack at transforming Iran is drifting along in the Persian Gulf, as on-again, off-again negotiations fail to resolve a conflict that has roiled the global economy while the president’s approval ratings plunge . Meanwhile, the Gaza Peace Plan is sinking , too, leaving ordinary Palestinians in a state of abject misery amid the rubble and tent cities of Gaza, cowering from Israeli air strikes that have killed more than 1,200 people since a “ceasefire” went into effect in Oct. 2025. To assess whether there’s a way out of these dismal situations, Responsible Statecraft spoke to Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), a potential 2028 presidential candidate who is known for being one of the Senate’s most vocal critics of Israeli conduct and of AIPAC’s influence on the Congress. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever. At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago Unesco reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening. items.summary: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever When a business makes long-term plans, they call it prudence. When a government makes long-term plans, they call it communism. Any sustained state intervention attracts the prefix “Soviet-style”, and triggers vicious attacks across the billionaire media. So governments have developed a bias against long-term thinking. This may explain why we no longer maintain strategic food reserves. In Britain, where soils have parched , market analysts warn that we’re facing the most severe food security crisis in decades. In normal years, crop failures at home don’t threaten our security, thanks to global trade. This is one of the reasons why hunger and famines are rarer and less deadly than they used to be. clusters.headline: Iran says no progress on reviving interim peace deal with US

items.title: Iran says no progress on reviving interim peace deal with US
items.summary: Iran says no progress on reviving interim peace deal with US Iran and the United States remain at loggerheads over efforts to agree on a permanent end to the war in the Gulf, according to a senior Iranian source, who said there had been no progress in talks to revive the interim deal agreed in June and define a timeframe to implement it. The comments came as US President Donald Trump issued yet another broadside against Iran's leaders, following new attacks on shipping in the region on Tuesday. The deal agreed in June declared an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts", but quickly unravelled, with Trump saying it was "over" on 7 July and Iran's foreign ministry declaring it "suspended" a week later. "One of the issues that is being discussed via mediators is the US returning to the interim agreement and defining a timeframe for implementing the commitments. There has been absolutely no progress on this issue," the Iranian source said.

Persbureau Reuters meldt dat de natuurramp waarschijnlijk ernstiger is dan de officiële berichten doen geloven. De olievlek zou inmiddels ruim 2000 vierkante kilometer groot zijn. clusters.headline: Pentagon says it killed at least 150 Yemeni civilians in strikes

items.title: Pentagon says it killed at least 150 Yemeni civilians in strikes
items.summary: The Pentagon acknowledged for the first time that U.S. military operations killed Yemeni civilians last year, in an annual report on civilian casualties it sent to members of Congress Tuesday. CENTCOM determined that three operations in Yemen last year “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm, the report said . It assessed that 153 civilians and wounded 243 others were killed as part of Operation Rough Rider, its campaign against Houthi targets in Yemen. The U.S. initially did not acknowledge that these operations, which were meant to stop the Houthis from attacking vessels in the Red Sea, killed civilians last year. The strikes included attacks on a port, a residential building, and a migrant detention center in Saada, where civilians were likely to be present. At the time, the U.S. limited the details it would disclose about its strikes, citing the need "to preserve operational security." items.title: Iran's new Security Council shake-up reveals growing divisions over US deal
items.summary: Iran's new Security Council shake-up reveals growing divisions over US deal Soon after Iranian negotiators reached a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States in late June to end months of hostilities, Iran 's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) issued a statement endorsing the agreement. The statement was signed by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a former hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) general who had replaced the slain Ali Larijani, a prominent moderate figure who had supported a deal with Washington and was killed in a US- Israeli strike on 17 March. In Iran, the SNSC secretary, who is appointed by the president, does not have a vote on the council. However, Zolghadr was also appointed simultaneously as the supreme leader’s representative on the council, a position that gives him voting authority. Zolghadr’s endorsement caught ultraconservative principlists off guard. clusters.headline: The Houthis could be first big test for Mecca mutual defense pact

items.title: The Houthis could be first big test for Mecca mutual defense pact
items.summary: When Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed their joint defense agreement in Mecca on August 7, the alliance’s first test was already taking shape. A day before the signing, Saudi Arabia was preparing for the possibility of attacks by the Houthis in Yemen alongside threats from Iran-linked groups in Iraq, amid concerns that energy facilities, ports, and airports could be targeted. The new pact establishes a striking principle: an armed attack on any one of the three countries is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. Yet what has been made public does not specify the military obligations that would follow, whether assistance would be automatic, or what form of response the other signatories would be expected to provide. So far, there are no indications that Turkey and Pakistan are preparing to enter the Yemen war directly. But a new Houthi missile or drone attack on Saudi Arabia could force the three countries to answer the question the agreement leaves unresolved: What does it actually mean to say that an attack on one is an attack on all? items.summary: Bij een aanval van de Houthi's op een vrachtschip in de Rode Zee gisteren zijn zes mensen om het leven gekomen. Dat meldt het transportministerie van Jemen. Het is voor het eerst sinds juli dat er doden vallen bij een Houthi-aanval op een schip. Het vrachtschip was vanaf de straat van Bab el-Mandeb onderweg richting de Rode Zee toen het volgens de regering van Jemen werd aangevallen met drie ballistische raketten. Het vrachtschip met de naam Timahah voer onder de vlag van Tanzania en is van een Egyptische eigenaar. Twee van de overleden slachtoffers waren leden van de militaire kustwacht van Jemen. De anderen waren drie Pakistanen en een Indonesiër, zegt het transportministerie. De Pakistaanse minister van Buitenlandse Zaken Ishaq Dar zegt de Houthi-aanval "ten zeerste" te veroordelen. items.summary: Bij Amerikaanse aanvallen op de Houthi's in Jemen vorig jaar zijn zeker 153 burgers om het leven gekomen en raakten bijna 250 burgers gewond. Dat blijkt uit een rapport van het ministerie van Defensie dat het jaarlijks moet delen met het Amerikaanse Congres. Vorig jaar voerde het Amerikaanse leger aanvallen uit op minstens duizend doelen van de Jemenitische militie. De strijdgroep heeft destijds zeker tientallen Amerikaanse defensievaartuigen en commerciële schepen in de Rode Zee onder vuur genomen. De Houthi's begonnen naar eigen zeggen met het uitvoeren van aanvallen in de Rode Zee uit solidariteit met de Palestijnen in Gaza. Ze hebben met de steun van Iran in grote delen van Jemen de macht en zijn tegen invloed van de VS en Israël in de regio. Burgerslachtoffers Volgens het leger gaat het in het rapport om slachtoffers die omkwamen bij drie Amerikaanse aanvallen. Bij een daarvan, op een gevangenis waar Afrikaanse migranten vastzaten, werden zeker 38 mensen gedood. Bij een andere aanval op een haven in Jemen vielen 80 doden. 71 mensen raakten daarbij gewond. items.summary: Israel and Venezuela restore diplomatic relations after years of severed ties Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 19:54 The rapprochement comes after the US has for months boasted of running Venezuela, following the capture of Maduro Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez speaks during a press conference at the Generalisimo Francisco de Miranda Air Base in Caracas, on 2 July 2026 (Lucas Agauyo/AFP) Off Israel and Venezuela announced the restoration of official diplomatic relations after 17 years of severed ties in mutual statements published on Tuesday. items.summary: Volgens president Trump is er niets aan de hand, maar in Amerika zijn grote zorgen ontstaan over de Amerikaanse wapenvoorraden. In de oorlog met Iran zou er een groot deel doorheen gejaagd zijn. Van sommige wapensystemen is nog maar 20 procent over. Luisteren? Deze aflevering van De Dag luister je via NPO Luister en alle andere podcastapps. Bevalt het? Vergeet je dan niet te abonneren. "Deze hele hoge verbruikscijfers gaan je voorstellingsvermogen te boven", zegt defensiespecialst Patrick Bolder van het Haags Centrum voor Strategische Studies in de podcast. "We hebben niet eerder gezien dat een grootmacht als Amerika zich eigenlijk laat verleiden om zoveel wapens te gebruiken dat ze er kwetsbaar door worden." Volgens hem ligt een gebrek aan strategie in combinatie met de inzet van AI om oorlogsdoelen aan te wijzen ten grondslag aan het probleem. Amerika-correspondent Sjoerd den Daas schetst hoe de Iran-oorlog steeds zwaarder op het presidentschap van Trump begint te drukken. items.summary: Iran condemns new US sanctions, calls them 'economic terrorism' Iran's foreign ministry condemned newly announced US economic and trade sanctions on Thursday, saying they targeted ordinary Iranians and amounted to "economic terrorism" and crimes against humanity. US President Donald Trump warned on Wednesday of sweeping economic consequences for any country that provided what he called "any type of lifeline to Iran", threatening economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale. items.summary: Een 17-jarige jongen die dit voorjaar een explosief liet afgaan bij een gebouw op de Amsterdamse Zuidas krijgt 165 dagen jeugddetentie, waarvan 122 voorwaardelijk. De explosie in maart van dit jaar was onderdeel van een reeks aanslagen op Amerikaanse en joodse doelwitten in Nederland en België. De verdachte gaf tijdens de zitting toe dat hij het explosief liet afgaan en zei dat hij dat deed voor geld. Hoeveel hij daarmee heeft verdiend is niet bekendgemaakt. Na de explosie werd op sociale media een filmpje verspreid waarin de aanslag werd opgeëist door een relatief onbekende organisatie. In het kantoorpand aan de Zuidas, dat overigens weinig schade opliep, is ook een Amerikaanse bank gevestigd. Terroristisch oogmerk niet bewezen De aanslagen lijken daarmee iets te maken te hebben met de oorlog die de VS en Israël waren gestart tegen Iran. Tijdens de inhoudelijke behandeling zei de officier van justitie dat hij niet kon bewijzen dat de verdachte een terroristisch oogmerk had. items.summary: Trump says US launching 'economic warfare' against Iran, warns countries not to back Tehran US President Donald Trump announced that the US is launching the "MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY". "This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale. Their navy is gone, their air force is destroyed, their military factories are now rubble, their currency is worthless, and their country is hanging by a thread," he said in a post on his platform Truth Social. The US president also warned that any country supporting Tehran in any way will face "TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences", but did not make mentions of a specific country or what actions Washington is expected to take. "This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat," he added. "These maniacs are on the ropes, and these HISTORIC MEASURES will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide. IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON."

Het aantal drone- en luchtaanvallen in Sudan is de afgelopen jaren sterk toegenomen: de Verenigde Naties telden in de eerste vier maanden van dit jaar 880 doden door droneaanvallen. Maandenlang was het relatief rustig in de hoofdstad Khartoem. Sinds het leger de stad vorig jaar weer in handen kreeg , proberen inwoners er een nieuw leven op te bouwen. Veel Sudanezen zijn teruggekeerd na jaren op de vlucht te zijn geweest. Maar afgelopen week werden burgers opnieuw opgeschrikt door een droneaanval. In Khartoem-Noord werd een moskee geraakt. "Ik lag te slapen op het dak van mijn huis", vertelt Noureddine Mohamed. "Het geluid was oorverdovend. Ik was bang dat de drone mijn huis zou raken. items.title: Iraq seeks special status for oil exports through Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iraq seeks special status for oil exports through Strait of Hormuz Iraq’s speaker of parliament has called for special status for the country’s oil exports passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Haibat al-Halbousi raised the request during talks with his Iranian counterpart, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, in Baghdad on Wednesday, according to a statement from his office. The statement did not explain what arrangements Baghdad wanted or whether Tehran had agreed to consider the proposal. The request highlights Iraq’s concern over the security of its energy exports as regional tensions increasingly threaten shipping through the critical waterway. The Strait of Hormuz connects the Gulf with the Arabian Sea and provides the main route for oil tankers leaving Iraq’s southern export terminals.

items.summary: NATO responds to alleged report that Iran considered targeting US forces in Europe NATO says it stands ready to defend all member states following a alleged report that Iran considered striking US military sites in Europe if President Donald Trump further escalates the war. An alliance official said on Wednesday that NATO would confront any danger and take whatever action it considered necessary to protect its members. "As demonstrated earlier this year when NATO air defences successfully intercepted ballistic missiles heading to Turkey from Iran on four separate occasions, our deterrence and defence posture is strong and effective," the official said. The comments followed a Financial Times report examining possible Iranian responses to further US military escalation. Washington maintains forces and bases across Europe.

items.title: Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On…
items.summary: The Iran war is beginning to resemble the Ukraine war in one important way. Operationally, the wars themselves are still very different — Ukraine is a large-scale ground invasion, while the Iran war is not there just yet. But their political logic after a failure to achieve a quick result is starting to look very similar. In both cases, a larger power expected its overwhelming military force to produce a quick political result. And in both cases, that expectation failed.The targeted state adapted, outside supporters helped it remain afloat, and both conflicts moved from the promise of a decisive outcome The post Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On… appeared first on War on the Rocks .

items.title: The Mecca Pact could be an opportunity for Iran
items.summary: The Mecca Pact ranks among the most momentous developments to have reshaped the Middle East since the upheavals that followed the Hamas attacks on October 7, 2023. Though defensive in nature, the agreement — which creates a mutual defense commitment between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey — could have major repercussions for the regional balance of power. Much hinges on how its signatories define the threats they must face and, more critically, on how other regional players, especially Iran and Israel, react to its creation. Although the pact has come into being amid the ongoing U.S.‑Iran confrontation, it need not be construed as an expressly anti‑Iran coalition. On the contrary, Tehran has good reason to view it favorably. The Turkish foreign minister indicated that preparations for the agreement had been underway for over two years . items.title: An independent Europe means no more US rooster in the henhouse
items.summary: NATO continues to prepare for life without the United States, at least as the dominant alliance member. “Europeans are already backfilling what the U.S. cannot any longer promise,” explained Secretary-General Mark Rutte . America's foreign policy establishmentarians have long worried about losing influence as a result. Indeed, by driving Europe away from America, Donald Trump may be inadvertently spurring creation of a serious counterweight to Washington. As CNN Fareed Zakaria warned : “As Europe’s spending increases, the continent will become less dependent on the U.S., and less deferential to it.” American policymakers, he added, might therefore regret the disappearance of the continent as a military backwater governed by obsequious nonentities, which served as a convenient base for U.S. troops to operate around the globe. The rise of Europe as an independent power will almost certainly transform international politics. And the process could be painful. items.title: US Justice Department targets Iranian institute for activity linked to IRGC
items.summary: US Justice Department targets Iranian institute for activity linked to IRGC The US Department of Justice (DoJ) announced charges on Tuesday against 17 members of Iran’s Mabna Institute for cyber activity and hacking “carried out on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other Iranian entities”. In a statement, the Department said Mabna Institute was involved in “a widespread cyber campaign”, which targeted over than 100,000 accounts belonging to university professors worldwide and stole more than 31 terabytes of academic and intellectual property data, along with email accounts belonging to employees. The campaign targeted 144 US universities and 178 foreign universities, at least 42 US companies and 11 foreign companies, as well as at least five US federal and local government agencies and two nongovernmental organisations, resulting in costs exceeding $20m, according to the statement.

The evaluation is being led by the Department of War’s policy office, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday, saying the war was viewed as “a once-in-a-generation chance for the Pentagon to reconsider its presence in the region”. The report said that the US has already signalled that it might not rebuild its bases attacked by Iran to pre-war status. The Washington Post corroborates Middle East Eye’s June report that cited current and former US officials as saying that a reckoning with the US’s old basing framework was expected as a result of the war. Former senior US officials have raised the prospect of a drawdown for months. El petróleo ha vuelto a subir, mientras las rentabilidades de la deuda pública alcanzan máximos de muchos años en Estados Unidos y varias economías europeas. El bono norteamericano a 30 años, un elemento clave de las carteras de renta fija a nivel mundial, está en su nivel más elevado desde 2007. Los inversores descuentan ya el riesgo de que la energía cara prolongue la inflación y obligue a mantener elevados los tipos de interés. It has become a struggle in which every side seeks to degrade their opponents, without achieving a victory the wider region cannot absorb. This makes Yemen an ideal test of an idea advanced by US strategist Edward Luttwak in his 1999 essay “ Give War a Chance ”, later applied to Syria in 2013: not every cessation of war constitutes peace, and not every victory produces a desirable outcome. items.title: The Iran war flushed $1.3 billion of Reaper drones down the drain
items.summary: The U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, worth at least $1.3 billion, since the start of its war on Iran, the Washington Post reported Friday . The drones can cost between $30 and $50 million each, depending on their sensor and weapons payload. The U.S. military has lost roughly 25% of its pre-war fleet in the past five months. A defense official told the Washington Post that some of the drones were not shot down by Iranian forces, but instead were lost after their communications link to their operators failed. They did not say how many were lost this way. Observers say the MQ-9 losses are par for the course amid a costly war with Iran. “The drip, drip, drip of this news shows how much the Trump administration is drawing down U.S. arsenals to support the war in Iran,” Justin Logan, the director of defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute, told RS. “First it was interceptors, then it was naval deployments, now it is drones, and tomorrow it will be something new.” “U.S. allies in the region know better, which is why, with the exception of Israel and partly the UAE, they

Since his first term, Trump has always been pessimistic about U.S.-South Korea joint exercises and has shown a flexible — and unpredictable — tendency toward them. items.title: Pentagon signs multibillion-dollar Tomahawk deal amid missile shortage concerns
items.summary: Pentagon signs multibillion-dollar Tomahawk deal amid missile shortage concerns The Pentagon announced a $22.9bn contract with Raytheon on Monday to accelerate deliveries of Tomahawk missiles, amid reports that US missile stocks have been strained by the war with Iran. Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the deal would speed up deliveries “at unprecedented speed” to meet current operational demands. A recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that US stocks of Patriot and THAAD interceptors have been cut by roughly half or more since the conflict with Iran began in late February. The Washington Post also reported that President Donald Trump had pressed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth for answers over munitions shortages, though both later denied that US missile stocks were running low. Tomahawk missiles are launched mainly from submarines and warships and have a range of more than 1,600km.

Iran bars two French diplomats from returning
items.summary: Iran bars two French diplomats from returning Iran said on Monday that two French diplomats briefly arrested last month over alleged “interference” would not be allowed to return to the country. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said the pair had left Iran and that Tehran had formally informed France they would be barred from re-entry. France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on 20 July that the diplomats had been targeted by Iranian security officials in violation of diplomatic immunity and described the incident as an “extremely serious act of intimidation”. Iran has accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs while engaging with civil society. Its intelligence ministry said they were involved in a broader effort to exert foreign influence, without providing further details. Tehran summoned the French ambassador on 26 July to protest against the diplomats’ conduct. Baqaei said on Monday that French authorities should apologise, arguing that the pair had violated the Vienna Convention.

items.summary: Houthis say they targeted Saudi military ship in Red Sea Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday that they had targeted a Saudi military vessel and four escort ships in the Red Sea with missiles. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree announced the attack on Telegram. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities. The reported attack comes days after the Houthis targeted a vessel near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Yemen’s transport ministry said four crew members were killed in that attack. The Bab el-Mandeb is a strategic maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for international shipping. In July, the Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, accusing Riyadh of imposing a siege on Yemen. Saudi Arabia has denied the allegation.

items.title: Iran says Hormuz transit route deal reached with Oman
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz transit route deal reached with Oman Iran on Monday said it has reached an understanding with Oman on a plan for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz, with the two sides now working to finalise details and issue a joint statement. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said “an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route”, adding that the agreement was being prepared as a package including the route map. Details that have previously emerged suggest ships could enter the strait along a route close to Iran and exit near Oman, without paying fees or tolls during an interim period. Baghaei acknowledged that negotiations had moved slowly but said Tehran and Muscat still planned to finalise the arrangement, as a deadline for a broader agreement between the United States and Iran expired without a deal.

items.title: Iran says 60-day deadline under US deal is no longer relevant
items.summary: Iran says 60-day deadline under US deal is no longer relevant Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said a 60-day period linked to the 17 June memorandum between Tehran and Washington was no longer relevant, accusing the United States of violating the agreement weeks after it was signed. “There is no provision in the memorandum of understanding referring to a ‘60-day deadline’, and the Islamic Republic of Iran never formulates its policies under pressure, ultimatums or time limits,” he said. Baghaei said the memorandum envisaged a 60-day period for talks on “the lifting of sanctions” and “the nuclear issue”, which could have been extended if no agreement was reached. However, he said “gross and widespread” US violations meant talks never began. “As a result, the issue of a 60-day deadline became entirely moot,” Baghaei added.

items.title: Stop gaslighting, USS Lincoln families didn't sign up for this
items.summary: The United States has always asked extraordinary things of its service members. But this week, a series of remarkable news stories came out documenting the dire conditions of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln , a ship that has been at sea so long that those aboard have not stepped foot on land since 2025. Even families like mine, who have experienced multiple combat deployments, are alarmed by the depictions we read in this news. We know that behind every sailor and Marine we read about on that ship, there is an entire family unit thousands of miles away wrestling with fear, exhaustion, confusion, anger, and loneliness every day that ship remains in harm’s way. From the spouses who suddenly became the only parent in their home, to the parents waiting anxiously for a phone call, to the children whose birthday parties and baseball games have an empty chair at them this year. items.title: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026
items.summary: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026 As the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, Iran struck back near US military installations in the Gulf, including in Qatar and the UAE. Several international airports were hit by Iranian strikes, including Dubai, the world's busiest for international passengers, as well as Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Bahrain. The UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait closed their airspaces due to safety concerns, gradually reopening them a week later as hostilities lessened. The war has had long-lasting consequences for regional aviation: falling passenger and cargo demand, fewer private jet flights, and global repercussions from high jet fuel prices. The International Air Transport Association's (IATA) June outlook estimated that airlines operating from the Middle East will see a $7.2bn net profit in 2025 become a $4.3bn net loss in 2026. Read more: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026

items.title: Opinion: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East
items.summary: Opinion: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East Nearly three years after the 7 October Hamas attack shattered the illusion of a manageable status quo - one serving US - Israeli interests, while harming Palestinian rights - and midway through President Donald Trump’s second term, the Middle East no longer maps neatly onto the two axes that have defined it for decades. The region’s fault line long ran between Iran ’s “Axis of Resistance” - comprising Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi armed groups, and a battered but defiant Syria under the Assad regime - and the Israeli-inspired “Pax Americana”: an informal architecture of deterrence, normalisation, and military primacy that Washington and Tel Aviv sought to impose through the Abraham Accords, blatant double standards, international law violations and overwhelming force. Today, a third pole could be emerging: an increasingly institutionalised “Sunni axis” anchored in Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad - with Doha, Cairo, and to a lesser extent Abu Dhabi at its edges. items.title: Iran resumes flights at Bandar Abbas airport after wartime disruptions
items.summary: Iran resumes flights at Bandar Abbas airport after wartime disruptions Flights at the port city of Bandar Abbas resumed on Saturday after repeated interruptions during war with the United States, state media reported. Kazem Tavassoli, director general of airports in Hormozgan province, said "scheduled flights at Bandar Abbas International Airport on high-traffic domestic routes resumed today, according to the IRNA state news agency. The reopening comes "following limited flights in recent days", Tavassoli said, adding that passengers can now buy tickets for the Tehran-Bandar Abbas, Mashhad-Bandar Abbas and Bandar Abbas-Isfahan routes, in both directions. The airport "handled 35 to 40 domestic and international flights per day" before the war, Tavassoli said. The airport has been repeatedly closed since the United States launched its war on Iran.

La nave trasportava circa 800 mila barili di petrolio russo e la chiazza avrebbe ormai superato i 2 mila chilometri quadrati, raggiungendo anche la costa dell’Oman. L’incidente minaccia una riserva marina protetta, habitat tra l’altro delle megattere del Mar Arabico e dei cormorani di Socotra. Trump’s remarks came as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said no decision has yet been made to resume negotiations with the United States. Araghchi added that mediator Qatar and Pakistan were in contact with Iran and exchanging messages, but that this did not amount to negotiations. Here are the latest developments from across the region: •    Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon early Saturday morning killed at least seven people. Advancing Israeli forces also demolished homes in Bint Jbeil. •    A bulk carrier has been struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz,  the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. •    Yemen’s government says at least four civilians were killed when Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of al-Mokha on Friday.

items.title: Oil climbs over $1 a barrel as expert warns of ‘day of reckoning’
items.summary: Oil climbs over $1 a barrel as expert warns of ‘day of reckoning’ Crude oil futures climbed over $1 a barrel on tanker attacks and a lack of progress on a peace agreement between the US and Iran. Reuters reported that Brent futures settled at $88.52 a barrel, up $1.45, or 1.67percent. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures finished at $82.40, up $1.15, or 1.42 percent. Brent and WTI were on track for weekly gains of 6.0 percent and 5.4 percent, respectively. "We're getting a rally going into the weekend after new attacks on tankers and lack of progress on a cease-fire agreement," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Reuters. A "day of reckoning" may come if traffic in the strait of Hormuz remains constrained, Lipow said. "Crude oil prices might be $80 a barrel, but diesel prices are $180 a barrel and gasoline is $130 a barrel and that's what's hitting the consumer," he added.

items.title: Trump urges Americans to accept higher oil prices
items.summary: Trump urges Americans to accept higher oil prices US President Donald Trump has urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices as the cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The comments underscore the growing political risk for Trump as higher fuel prices collide with his campaign promise to lower energy costs, with Democrats already seeking to make the economic fallout from the Iran war an issue heading into the November midterm elections. In a speech in Garden City, Trump said Americans who had to "pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" should remember that this was the cost of ensuring "a very evil country" could not have a nuclear weapon. "What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a great job," said Trump, adding he would never apologize for attacking Iran. Around roughly 20 percent of global oil and LNG shipments usually pass through the Strait of Hormuz and the potential for long-term disruption has pushed up oil prices. (Reporting by Reuters)

items.summary: Hormuz traffic rises from nine to 13 crossings, Kpler says Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz increased on 13 August, with 13 confirmed vessel crossings, up 44 percent from nine crossings recorded the previous day, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. Nine vessels used Iran's unilateral transit scheme, while no vessels were confirmed on the Hormuz Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS). The routes of four other vessels remained undetermined. Activity through the Bab el-Mandeb was steadier, with 29 confirmed crossings, up 4 percent from 28 the previous day. Eighteen vessels entered the Red Sea and 11 exited, while two dark transits were recorded. No new confirmed vessel attacks were reported during the day, Kpler added. items.title: Araghchi says talks with Oman about Strait of Hormuz ‘may reach conclusion soon’
items.summary: Araghchi says talks with Oman about Strait of Hormuz ‘may reach conclusion soon’ Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that negotiations between Iran and Oman “may reach a conclusion soon,” Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) reported. Araghchi said the talks with Oman regarding the shared management of the Strait of Hormuz between the two countries “are ongoing, but this is a completely separate discussion” from ceasefire talks with the United States. He added that “a technical discussion related to determining the maritime routes of the Strait of Hormuz for ship traffic” is continuing. “This is a technical work that is being done between experts from the two countries and the armed forces are also involved in it,” Araghchi said. “In any case, they are the main opinion leaders on this issue.”

items.title: Vance says low oil prices are top US goal in Iran conflict
items.summary: Vance says low oil prices are top US goal in Iran conflict Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that the top US priority in the Iran war was keeping oil and gasoline prices low for Americans, with preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon ranking second. The remarks contrasted with President Donald Trump's repeated framing of the fight: that entering the war had the sole objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, even if that meant short-term economic sacrifices for Americans. Vance's comments also underscored the growing reality that the war now centres on control of the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has forced to the top of the negotiating agenda. "I know that oil is down today and it's way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict," Vance said on Fox News. "That's goal number one - keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country." "And then obviously goal number two is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon," he added.

items.title: US has lost roughly 25 percent of its Reaper drones in Iran war: Report
items.summary: US has lost roughly 25 percent of its Reaper drones in Iran war: Report The US-Israeli war on Iran has depleted or destroyed more than $1.3bn worth of the US's MQ-9 Reaper drones, roughly translating to 25 percent of the country's pre-war fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a report by The Washington Post published on Friday. The report underscores how Iran's air defences have continued to be operational despite claims by President Donald Trump and his aides that they have been obliterated. The Washington Post story reveals a slightly higher number of MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed compared to a Bloomberg report published in May, which put the figure at 20 percent of the pre-war inventory. The MQ-9 Reaper drone is valued between $30m and $50m, depending on its sensor, radar, and ordnance configuration. The unmanned aerial vehicle serves as a high-altitude platform for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeted precision strikes, as documented by the US Air Force . Asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation on the Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, Trump said: "No, they're not." Trump also rejected that the ship - now in its ninth month at sea - had been deployed for too long. "No, no, no, not nearly enough," he said. Trump confirmed reports that the Abraham Lincoln was due to be rotated with a replacement aircraft carrier as the United States remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz and the country's nuclear programme. "That ship is moving right now or very shortly, and it's being replaced with another very similar ship," Trump said.

The Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days without a port call. At least one sailor jumped overboard the vessel, and another had to be restrained from doing so, according to media reports. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Lincoln will be rotated out of the theatre of operations and replaced with the USS George Washington. US lawmakers have raised concerns about the physical and mental health of sailors on board. The rotation comes after US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said that the blockade of Iran can be conducted “indefinitely”, as fighting continues to rage for control over the Strait of Hormuz with no return to a ceasefire in sight. Valiullah Bayati, a spokesperson for the parliament’s internal affairs and councils committee, said on Friday that the proposals would now advance for further consideration. “The strategic action plan to ensure the security and progress of the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf was reviewed by the Councils’ Commission and, after hearing the opinions, its general outline was approved,” said Bayati to the Tasnim news agency . The plan would prevent vessels and equipment belonging to the US, Israel and other countries Iran designates as hostile from passing through the waterway. items.summary: Door de oorlog in Iran en de hogere energieprijzen dreigen veel Nederlandse huishoudens in 2027 minder te besteden te krijgen. De koopkracht daalt met 0,3 procent als de overheid het beleid ongewijzigd laat. Dit jaar stijgt de koopkracht voor de doorsnee Nederlander nog wel, maar een stuk minder dan tot nu toe werd verwacht. In de laatste berekening ging het CBP er nog van uit dat dit jaar de koopkracht met 1,4 procent zou stijgen. Dat is bijgesteld naar 0,6 procent. Dat blijkt uit de nieuwste ramingen van het Centraal Planbureau (CPB) in de Macro-Economische Verkenningen (MEV). Die worden gezien als het uitgangspunt voor de onderhandelingen tussen politieke partijen over de Miljoenennota. Het kabinet kan, in samenwerking met de oppositie, maatregelen nemen om bepaalde groepen te compenseren. Toch vallen de gevolgen mee als je ziet wat er aan de hand is in de wereld, stelt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Over de hele linie valt het mee. De Nederlandse economie is veerkrachtig." Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history | Simon Jenkins
items.summary: It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too Wars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever. At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago Unesco reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening. items.title: Britain's scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help | George Monbiot
items.summary: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever When a business makes long-term plans, they call it prudence. When a government makes long-term plans, they call it communism. Any sustained state intervention attracts the prefix “Soviet-style”, and triggers vicious attacks across the billionaire media. So governments have developed a bias against long-term thinking. This may explain why we no longer maintain strategic food reserves. In Britain, where soils have parched , market analysts warn that we’re facing the most severe food security crisis in decades. In normal years, crop failures at home don’t threaten our security, thanks to global trade. This is one of the reasons why hunger and famines are rarer and less deadly than they used to be. But this is not a normal year, because the problem is now global. Continue reading...
